Abstract\u2014Few decisions shape a life as much as the choice of what to study and which career to pursue, yet good guidance remains unevenly distributed. Personal mentoring is scarce and costly, while the tools most job seekers actually reach for\u2014aptitude quizzes, keyword-driven job boards and generic advice columns\u2014seldom account for who the individual really is. Large language models (LLMs) can hold fluent, mentor-like conversations, but on their own they fabricate facts, fall behind a fast-moving labour market and reason only shallowly about a person's background. This paper describes a career development assistant that closes these gaps by pairing an instruction-tuned LLM with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The assistant indexes a curated knowledge base\u2014occupation profiles drawn from the National Classification of Occupations (NCO-2015), skill taxonomies, learning resources and current job postings\u2014and retrieves supporting passages to ground every reply. Four capabilities sit behind a single retrieve-then-generate core: skill-gap analysis, learning-path recommendation, resume and interview feedback, and job-fit explanation. We present the architecture, the profile-aware retrieval and grounding strategy, and a serving design suited to interactive use. Across offline evaluation and a user study, grounding raises answer faithfulness and recommendation relevance while sharply lowering hallucination relative to an LLM-only baseline, indicating that retrieval is a practical foundation for career guidance that people can actually trust.\nIndex Terms\u2014Large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, career guidance, recommender systems, personalization, question answering, natural language processing

\n \n \n OBJECTIVE\n

What to study, which skills to build, which roles to chase\u2014these choices follow a person for years, shaping their earnings, their stability and their sense of purpose. Access to sound advice about them, however, is deeply unequal. One-to-one mentoring is expensive and in short supply, and the resources that fill the gap for most people\u2014static aptitude quizzes, keyword-driven job boards and one-size-fits-all articles\u2014rarely reflect an individual's history, constraints or the reality of the market they are trying to enter.
